topic.title: Yours, mine, ours: the separate-accounts marriage
topic.claim: Keeping money separate feels like a fair, modern deal until a crisis shows you were running two households with one address.
topic.behaviour: Dual-income couples keep finances completely separate, assuming it all balances out. Then a health emergency, a family wedding or a job scare exposes the gap in savings and security.
topic.mechanism: Separate money signals independence and fairness. Underneath is a fear of dependence, and a belief that sharing means losing control.
real_details: A thread by a 37-year-old describes a household with two high salaries and completely separate finances
A large unexpected medical expense for a newborn was mostly covered by office insurance, but savings stopped
The poster realised savings and assets between spouses were very uneven despite similar incomes
Commenters said the real issue was stress and the emotional phase after a child, not money
One commenter said money belongs to both partners and that fighting is a sign something else is wrong
topic.why_now: Festival and wedding spending season is when couples quietly compare what each side has, so the question lands now.

score.reason: clears mirror and freshness bars — a real, under-discussed couple's blind spot
score.best_hook: Two salaries, two accounts, one address. It works — until one month something goes wrong for both of you.
